name: halowars
title: Halo Wars: Definitive Edition

ready_sequence.note: Microsoft and 343 logos, then an attract reel behind the 'Press any key or button to continue' title screen, which is up about 21 s after launch
A clears the title screen; the main menu follows within about 5 s
d-pad down from CAMPAIGN to SKIRMISH; a cold launch always opens with CAMPAIGN highlighted
A accepts SKIRMISH and opens the lobby
START GAME is the Start button, not A: the lobby's own footer says so. The defaults are already a playable 1v1 (CHASMS, STANDARD, AUTOMATIC difficulty 40), so nothing needs editing
the match is fully loaded and idle within 10 s of the press; 25 is the safe margin

notes:
Halo Wars: Definitive Edition (2016, Ensemble/Behaviour), the fifth game in the harness and the first real-time strategy one. No anti-cheat, so it starts under test signing, and no console, so the oracle is the frame one: verdicts come from measured motion (a shift, and with motion.kind rotate a rotation and a zoom, beside a change grid) against thresholds from three idle seconds; there is a button reset (below) but no calibration table, as for Elden Ring and PowerWash Simulator. The rotation estimate recovers nothing on a one-second swing at 0.60 and above (the camera goes past the overlap), so those steps are MOVED by the whole-picture rule; a degrees table would need shorter holds. Runs borderless fullscreen at the desktop resolution (2560x1440 here) on its own; the recipe's window key puts it at 1280x720 borderless, which it accepted in one call on 2026-09-09 and then came up at itself on the next launch. The window title is exactly 'Halo Wars: Definitive Edition' and the process is xgameFinal.exe.

What an RTS does to the harness's assumptions, all confirmed against the game's own CONTROL DIAGRAM screen (pause, then the third entry): there is no player and no camera to look with, so the checks measure a *camera* rather than a view. The left stick is CAMERA, which scrolls the map, and the cursor stays fixed near the middle of the screen instead of moving with it. The right stick is ROTATE CAMERA: rx swings the camera around the map point it is over, and ry zooms in and out. That is a lucky fit rather than a designed one, because rx is the axis the yaw checks (G4, G5, G6) drive and rotation does not translate the camera, so those checks always measure the same scene. Only G8's second of left stick moves the camera off the base. A is SELECT, B is CANCEL, X is ATTACK, Y is ABILITY, Back is OBJECTIVES and Start is PAUSE GAME. The d-pad jumps the camera: left to BASES (measured), the others to ARMIES, ALERTS and POWERS. LT is FAST SCROLL, a *modifier* for the left stick rather than an action of its own, which is why holding it alone changed 16 samples of 102,480 and reads as a dead trigger; RT is SUB-SELECT UNITS and RB is LOCAL, both no-ops with nothing selected.

The skirmish base view is the quietest scene of any game in the harness: an idle second changes about 600 to 950 samples of 102,480, and two captures 28 s apart differed by 676, against PowerWash Simulator's 1259 floor and Elden Ring's 330 to 456. Nothing in an RTS base animates much. That makes the frame verdicts unusually trustworthy here.

The menus are highlight-driven, not pointer-driven, so this recipe needs none of PowerWash Simulator's `pointer` machinery: the d-pad walks a highlight and A accepts. Two things about them cost time to learn. **The menus wrap**, so there is no walking to a known end and counting down from it: four presses of d-pad down from the pause menu's CONTROL DIAGRAM landed on OPTIONS, having passed the bottom and come round. The sequence therefore depends on the main menu opening with CAMPAIGN highlighted, which is what a cold launch does. **The readiness stick test cannot be used at all here**, which is why this recipe is fixed waits and blind presses where Elden Ring's and PowerWash Simulator's are `press_until_control`: the title screen plays a full-screen attract reel, so a stick test against the picture reports MOVED on the title screen and would declare the game ready in a menu. A game whose menus are animated needs a timed sequence, and the timings above have about a threefold margin.

Why pressing A blindly is safe: a skirmish against an AI is a sandbox with no save to damage and no confirm dialog to trip. In world A selects and X attacks, and with nothing selected both do nothing at all (35 and 87 samples). The harness kills the process at the end and the match is discarded, so a run leaves nothing behind. Difficulty AUTOMATIC (40) and a four-minute run mean the AI never gets near the base.

**There is a real reset here, and reset_buttons uses it.** d-pad left jumps the camera to the base and right-stick click puts the rotation back to north, so pressing 13 then 10 restores the opening view from anywhere on the map. The first reset's picture is the reference frame and every later reset is measured against it (G2: a second of left stick scrolls the camera off, the buttons bring it back, the motion from the reference reads STILL; landing at static 0.97 on the pad run and 0.99 through Nimbus, 2026-09-09). Frame verdicts are motion verdicts now, and the one that mattered flipped: through Nimbus the 0.289 floor reads STILL, so floor_moves_camera is false and N2 checks that the bridge sent its floor and the camera did not move, the measured property of this game.

One game setting scales what the harness measures: OPTIONS > CONTROLS > Scroll Speed, a slider that sets how fast the left stick scrolls the camera, at about three quarters of the way to Fast on this install. Camera Rotation, Default Zoom and Crosshair Stickiness sit beside it, and Input Device reads Gamepad once a pad exists at launch. Rerun this recipe after changing any of them.
